claim: Histones are a principal constituent of chromatin in eukaryotes and fundamental to our understanding of eukaryotic gene regulation.
source: Histones are a principal constituent of chromatin in eukaryotes and fundamental to our understanding of eukaryotic gene regulation.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific consensus about the role of histones in eukaryotes.

claim: In archaea, histones are widespread but not universal: several lineages have lost histone genes.
source: In archaea, histones are widespread but not universal: several lineages have lost histone genes.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work in the literature.

claim: Thermoplasma acidophilum harbors a HU family protein (HTa) that protects part of the genome from micrococcal nuclease digestion.
source: Here, we elucidate primary chromatin architecture in an archaeon without histones, Thermoplasma acidophilum, which harbors a HU family protein (HTa) that protects part of the genome from micrococcal nuclease digestion.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript and cited prior work.

claim: HTa preferentially binds to GC-rich sequences.
source: HTa preferentially binds to GC-rich sequences, exhibits invariant positioning throughout the growth cycle, and shows archaeal histone-like oligomerization behavior.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from MNase-seq, in vitro reconstitution, and EMSA experiments presented in the manuscript.

claim: HTa exhibits invariant positioning throughout the growth cycle.
source: HTa preferentially binds to GC-rich sequences, exhibits invariant positioning throughout the growth cycle, and shows archaeal histone-like oligomerization behavior.
evidence: This is supported by MNase-seq data across different growth phases showing stable peak locations.

claim: HTa shows archaeal histone-like oligomerization behavior.
source: HTa preferentially binds to GC-rich sequences, exhibits invariant positioning throughout the growth cycle, and shows archaeal histone-like oligomerization behavior.
evidence: This is supported by analysis of fragment size distributions and coverage patterns showing nested, edge-aligned structures similar to archaeal histones.

claim: HTa is a DNA-binding protein of bacterial origin.
source: Our results suggest that HTa, a DNA-binding protein of bacterial origin, has converged onto an architectural role filled by histones in other archaea.
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis showing HTa was acquired via horizontal gene transfer from bacteria.

claim: HTa has converged onto an architectural role filled by histones in other archaea.
source: Our results suggest that HTa, a DNA-binding protein of bacterial origin, has converged onto an architectural role filled by histones in other archaea.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from multiple lines of experimental evidence showing histone-like properties of HTa.

claim: Eukaryotic histones assemble into octameric complexes that wrap approximately 147 bp of DNA.
source: Assembling into octameric complexes that wrap ~ 147 bp of DNA, eukaryotic histones not only mediate genome compaction but also establish a basal landscape of differential accessibility, elaborated via a plethora of post-translational modifications, that is fundamental to our understanding of eukaryotic gene regulation (Jiang and Pugh, 2009; Bai and Morozov, 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge about eukaryotic histones, supported by citations.

claim: Archaeal histones have the same core fold as eukaryotic histones.
source: They have the same core fold (Decanniere et al., 2000; Mattiroli et al., 2017) as eukaryotic histones, but lack N- and typically also C-terminal tails, the principal substrates for post-translational modifications in eukaryotes (Henneman et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to structural studies.

claim: Archaeal histones lack N- and typically also C-terminal tails.
source: They have the same core fold (Decanniere et al., 2000; Mattiroli et al., 2017) as eukaryotic histones, but lack N- and typically also C-terminal tails, the principal substrates for post-translational modifications in eukaryotes (Henneman et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Archaeal histones are dimers in solution and assemble into tetramers that wrap approximately 60 bp of DNA.
source: Dimers in solution, they assemble into tetramers that wrap ~ 60 bp of DNA (Bailey et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The minimal nucleosomal unit of archaeal histones can be extended into a longer oligomer via incorporation of additional dimers in some archaea.
source: This minimal nucleosomal unit can be extended, at least in some archaea, into a longer oligomer via incorporation of additional dimers (Xie and Reeve, 2004; Maruyama et al., 2013; Mattiroli et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Archaeal nucleosomes preferentially bind sequences that facilitate wrapping, for example by means of periodically spaced GC/GG/AA/TT dinucleotides.
source: Like their eukaryotic counterparts, archaeal nucleosomes preferentially bind sequences that facilitate wrapping, for example by means of periodically spaced GC/GG/AA/TT dinucleotides (Bailey and Reeve, 1999; Bailey et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: On average, nucleosome occupancy is higher on more GC-rich sequences and lower around transcriptional start and end sites in archaea.
source: On average, nucleosome occupancy is higher on more GC-rich sequences and lower around transcriptional start and end sites (Ammar et al., 2011; Nalabothula et al., 2013), which tend to be AT-rich.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Archaeal histones have been deleted experimentally in several species without dramatic effects on transcription and growth.
source: Although widespread, archaeal histones are less entrenched than histones in eukaryotes: they have been deleted experimentally in several species without dramatic effects on transcription and growth (Heinicke et al., 2004; Weidenbach et al., 2008; Dulmage et al., 2015) and lost altogether from a handful of archaeal lineages (Adam et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior experimental work.

claim: Archaeal histones have been lost altogether from a handful of archaeal lineages.
source: Although widespread, archaeal histones are less entrenched than histones in eukaryotes: they have been deleted experimentally in several species without dramatic effects on transcription and growth (Heinicke et al., 2004; Weidenbach et al., 2008; Dulmage et al., 2015) and lost altogether from a handful of archaeal lineages (Adam et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Thermoplasma acidophilum lacks histone genes.
source: A particularly intriguing case concerns the thermophilic acidophile Thermoplasma acidophilum, which lacks histone genes but instead encodes a protein named HTa (Histone-like protein of Thermoplasma acidophilum).
evidence: This is established knowledge about T. acidophilum genome content.

claim: HTa is a member of the HU family of proteins based on its primary sequence and predicted secondary, tertiary and quaternary structure.
source: Based on its primary sequence (DeLange et al., 1981; Drlica and Rouviere-Yaniv, 1987) and predicted secondary, tertiary and quaternary structure (Figure 1a–b), HTa is a member of the HU family of proteins.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work and structural predictions shown in Figure 1.

claim: The average E. coli cell during exponential growth contains an estimated 30,000–55,000 HU molecules.
source: As in E. coli, where the average cell during exponential growth contains an estimated 30,000–55,000 HU molecules (Figure 1c; Ali Azam et al., 1999), HU proteins are often abundant constituents of bacterial chromatin.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work and data shown in Figure 1c.

claim: HU proteins are broadly distributed across bacterial phyla.
source: They are also frequently essential (Grove, 2011) and broadly distributed across bacterial phyla (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by citation and data in supplementary file.

claim: HU proteins are comparatively rare outside bacteria.
source: Outside bacteria, HU proteins are comparatively rare (Figure 2a).
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 2a.

claim: HU proteins are found with phylogenetic persistence only in some single-celled eukaryotes and in a single clade of archaea: the Thermoplasmatales/DHVE2 group.
source: They are found with a modicum of phylogenetic persistence only in some single-celled eukaryotes, where they are known to play important functional roles (Sasaki et al., 2009; Gornik et al., 2012), and in a single clade of archaea: the Thermoplasmatales/deep-sea hydrothermal vent euryarchaeota (DHVE2 group).
evidence: This is supported by citations and phylogenetic analysis.

claim: HTa was acquired via horizontal gene transfer from bacteria at the root of the Thermoplasmatales/DHVE2 clade.
source: Phylogenetic reconstruction of the HTa/HU gene family suggests that HTa was acquired via horizontal gene transfer from bacteria at the root of this clade (Figure 2b, see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 2b.

claim: HTa is highly abundant in T. acidophilum.
source: In T. acidophilum, HTa is highly abundant (Figure 1c) and protects ~ 25–35% of the genome from micrococcal nuclease (MNase) digestion (Searcy and Stein, 1980; Thomm et al., 1982), consistent with a global role in structuring T. acidophilum chromatin.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1c and citations to prior work.

claim: HTa protects approximately 25–35% of the T. acidophilum genome from micrococcal nuclease digestion.
source: In T. acidophilum, HTa is highly abundant (Figure 1c) and protects ~ 25–35% of the genome from micrococcal nuclease (MNase) digestion (Searcy and Stein, 1980; Thomm et al., 1982), consistent with a global role in structuring T. acidophilum chromatin.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: MNase digestion of native T. acidophilum chromatin yields two distinct fragment sizes of approximately 40 bp and approximately 80 bp.
source: Pioneering work by Searcy and colleagues showed that MNase digestion of native T. acidophilum chromatin yields two distinct fragment sizes of ~ 40 bp and ~ 80 bp (Searcy and Stein, 1980).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: MNase digestion of calf thymus DNA following in vitro reconstitution with purified HTa produces a similar banding pattern to native T. acidophilum chromatin.
source: The same authors observed a similar banding pattern when they digested calf thymus DNA following in vitro reconstitution with purified HTa, suggesting that native HTa is sufficient for and likely the principal mediator of protection from MNase digestion in T. acidophilum (Searcy and Stein, 1980).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: MNase treatment coupled to high-throughput sequencing reveals footprints of protection throughout the T. acidophilum genome.
source: Using MNase treatment coupled to high-throughput sequencing, we find footprints of protection throughout the genome.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: MNase digestion of T. acidophilum chromatin shows a bimodal distribution of protected fragment sizes.
source: Confirming prior results (Searcy and Stein, 1980), we observe a bimodal distribution of protected fragment sizes and subsequently infer small and large binding footprints.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3 and citations to prior work.

claim: The smaller HTa footprints are well predicted by simple sequence features.
source: The more common smaller footprints are well predicted by simple sequence features and display a general preference for GC-rich sequences.
evidence: This is supported by LASSO modeling and sequence analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: HTa displays the same sequence preferences in an HTa-expressing E. coli strain as in T. acidophilum.
source: We observe the same preferences in an HTa-expressing E. coli strain, when we reconstitute chromatin using purified HTa and T. acidophilum genomic DNA, and in electrophoretic mobility shift assays (EMSAs) of GC-variable DNA oligos, consistent with sequence as a key determinant of HTa binding in vivo.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from E. coli MNase-seq, in vitro reconstitution, and EMSA experiments.

claim: HTa displays the same sequence preferences when chromatin is reconstituted using purified HTa and T. acidophilum genomic DNA as in vivo.
source: We observe the same preferences in an HTa-expressing E. coli strain, when we reconstitute chromatin using purified HTa and T. acidophilum genomic DNA, and in electrophoretic mobility shift assays (EMSAs) of GC-variable DNA oligos, consistent with sequence as a key determinant of HTa binding in vivo.
evidence: This is supported by in vitro reconstitution experiments.

claim: HTa displays the same sequence preferences in electrophoretic mobility shift assays of GC-variable DNA oligos as in vivo.
source: We observe the same preferences in an HTa-expressing E. coli strain, when we reconstitute chromatin using purified HTa and T. acidophilum genomic DNA, and in electrophoretic mobility shift assays (EMSAs) of GC-variable DNA oligos, consistent with sequence as a key determinant of HTa binding in vivo.
evidence: This is supported by EMSA experiments.

claim: Larger HTa-protected fragments are frequently derived from nucleation-extension events akin to oligomerization of archaeal histones.
source: In addition, we present evidence that larger fragments are frequently derived from nucleation-extension events akin to oligomerization of archaeal histones (Maruyama et al., 2013; Nalabothula et al., 2013; Mattiroli et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of fragment coverage patterns and citations to prior work on archaeal histone oligomerization.

claim: MNase digestion of T. acidophilum yielded protected fragments of two distinct sizes throughout the growth cycle.
source: Throughout, MNase digestion yielded protected fragments of two distinct sizes (Figure 3b), in line with previous results (Searcy and Stein, 1980).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3b and citation to prior work.

claim: MNase digestion of E. coli cells expressing recombinant HTa produced a protection pattern very similar to T. acidophilum.
source: MNase digestion of E. coli cells expressing recombinant HTa produced a very similar protection pattern (Figure 3c).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3c.

claim: HTa readily binds DNA outside its native cellular environment.
source: This demonstrates that HTa readily binds DNA outside its native cellular environment and does not require T. acidophilum-specific post-translational modifications or binding partners to protect from MNase digestion, consistent with previous in vitro reconstitution experiments (Searcy and Stein, 1980).
evidence: This is inferred from the E. coli expression experiment and supported by citation to prior work.

claim: HTa does not require T. acidophilum-specific post-translational modifications or binding partners to protect from MNase digestion.
source: This demonstrates that HTa readily binds DNA outside its native cellular environment and does not require T. acidophilum-specific post-translational modifications or binding partners to protect from MNase digestion, consistent with previous in vitro reconstitution experiments (Searcy and Stein, 1980).
evidence: This is inferred from the E. coli expression experiment and supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Native E. coli HU (HupA) does not confer significant protection under equivalent digestion conditions when strongly over-expressed from the same plasmid.
source: In contrast, native E. coli HU (HupA), even when strongly over-expressed from the same plasmid, does not confer significant protection under equivalent digestion conditions (Figure 3c).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3c.

claim: HU orthologs from Thermobacillus composti and Lactobacillus floricola do not confer significant protection under equivalent digestion conditions.
source: Neither do HU orthologs from Thermobacillus composti and Lactobacillus floricola (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), which have higher sequence identity to HTa (37% and 39% compared to 27% for E. coli HupA).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: HTa is unusual among HU family proteins in its capacity to protect DNA from MNase attack.
source: HTa is therefore unusual, although perhaps not unique (Ghosh and Grove, 2004; Mukherjee et al., 2008) among HU family proteins in its capacity to protect DNA from MNase attack.
evidence: This is inferred from comparison with other HU proteins and supported by citations.

claim: Two major fragment size classes are present across all stages of the T. acidophilum growth cycle.
source: Next, we sequenced the T. acidophilum DNA fragments that survived MNase treatment (see Materials and methods). As anticipated, two major fragment size classes are present across all stages of the growth cycle (Figure 3d, Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by sequencing data shown in Figure 3d and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Small fragments are defined as 40–65 bp in size.
source: For downstream analysis, we define small (large) fragments as 40–65 bp (70–100 bp) in size and note the following:
evidence: This is a methodological definition based on observed fragment size distributions.

claim: Large fragments are defined as 70–100 bp in size.
source: For downstream analysis, we define small (large) fragments as 40–65 bp (70–100 bp) in size and note the following:
evidence: This is a methodological definition based on observed fragment size distributions.

claim: Genome-wide occupancy of 70–80 bp and 80–90 bp fragments is highly correlated (Spearman's ρ = 0.76, p<2.2e-16).
source: However, genome-wide occupancy of 70–80 bp and 80–90 bp fragments is highly correlated (Spearman's ρ = 0.76, p<2.2e-16, Figure 3e) and we therefore consider 70–80 bp and 80–90 bp fragments jointly.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of sequencing data shown in Figure 3e.

claim: Modal fragment sizes in this study (~50 bp and ~ 85 bp) are slightly larger than those reported previously (~40 bp and ~ 80 bp).
source: Second, modal fragment sizes (~50 bp and ~ 85 bp) are slightly larger than those reported previously (~40 bp and ~ 80 bp) (Searcy and Stein, 1980).
evidence: This is based on comparison of current data with cited prior work.

claim: The difference in modal fragment sizes compared to prior work reflects digestion conditions.
source: At least in part, this reflects digestion conditions: fragments obtained after doubling digestion time from 15 to 30 min are shorter and map inside larger footprints (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: Protection across the T. acidophilum genome is both ubiquitous and heterogeneous.
source: We then mapped fragments, irrespective of their size, to the T. acidophilum genome (see Materials and methods). Protection across the genome is both ubiquitous and heterogeneous, with relatively even coverage along the origin-terminus axis once increased copy number of early replicating regions is taken into account (see Materials and methods, Figure 3f–g).
evidence: This is supported by genome-wide mapping data shown in Figure 3f-g.

claim: Major drop-offs in MNase coverage correspond to areas of low GC content.
source: Major drop-offs in coverage correspond to areas of low GC content, as evident from Figure 3f, formally shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4, and further explored below.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3f and Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: Genome-wide occupancy is highly correlated across replicates for any given growth phase (mean ρ = 0.89, p<2.2e-16 for all pairwise comparisons).
source: For any given growth phase, genome-wide occupancy is highly correlated across replicates (mean ρ = 0.89, p<2.2e-16 for all pairwise comparisons).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of replicate data.

claim: Peak locations vary little across the T. acidophilum growth cycle.
source: Globally, peak locations vary little across the growth cycle (Figure 3h).
evidence: This is supported by peak overlap analysis shown in Figure 3h.

claim: 13,915 narrow peaks were observed in exponential phase (day 2).
source: Below, we will focus on data from exponential phase (day 2), where we observe 13,915 narrow and 6887 broad peaks, before discussing variability of HTa-mediated chromatin architecture across the growth cycle in the context of transcriptional changes.
evidence: This is based on peak calling analysis of MNase-seq data.

claim: 6887 broad peaks were observed in exponential phase (day 2).
source: Below, we will focus on data from exponential phase (day 2), where we observe 13,915 narrow and 6887 broad peaks, before discussing variability of HTa-mediated chromatin architecture across the growth cycle in the context of transcriptional changes.
evidence: This is based on peak calling analysis of MNase-seq data.

claim: Small and large fragments often overlap at called peaks.
source: Considering read coverage around called peaks, it is evident that small and large fragments often overlap (Figure 3g, Figure 4c,f), indicating the presence of different protective entities in the same location across cells.
evidence: This is supported by coverage analysis shown in Figure 3g and Figure 4c,f.

claim: Broad peaks are typically a combination of small and large fragments.
source: Importantly, broad peaks are typically a combination of small and large fragments and often show asymmetric coverage (caused by smaller fragments) around the summit of the inferred peak (see Figure 4a for an example).
evidence: This is supported by coverage analysis shown in Figure 4a.

claim: Broad peaks often show asymmetric coverage around the summit of the inferred peak.
source: Importantly, broad peaks are typically a combination of small and large fragments and often show asymmetric coverage (caused by smaller fragments) around the summit of the inferred peak (see Figure 4a for an example).
evidence: This is supported by coverage analysis shown in Figure 4a.

claim: Some archaeal histones can form oligomers.
source: Given that some archaeal histones (Maruyama et al., 2013; Mattiroli et al., 2017) and bacterial HU proteins (Hammel et al., 2016; Hołówka et al., 2017) can form oligomers, we reasoned that asymmetric coverage might contain valuable information about the potential genesis of larger fragments from smaller nucleation sites.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Some bacterial HU proteins can form oligomers.
source: Given that some archaeal histones (Maruyama et al., 2013; Mattiroli et al., 2017) and bacterial HU proteins (Hammel et al., 2016; Hołówka et al., 2017) can form oligomers, we reasoned that asymmetric coverage might contain valuable information about the potential genesis of larger fragments from smaller nucleation sites.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Smaller fragments are aligned to the edge rather than the center of broad-peak footprints.
source: To retain this signal, lost when averaging over individual peaks in aggregate plots, we re-oriented the coverage signal as displayed in Figure 4b, revealing that smaller fragments are aligned to the edge – rather than the center – of broad-peak footprints (Figure 4d,g).
evidence: This is supported by re-oriented coverage analysis shown in Figure 4d,g.

claim: M. fervidus shows a very similar nested, edge-aligned structure of smaller fragments within broader peaks as T. acidophilum.
source: We then applied the same procedure to MNase-Seq data we had independently generated for the histone-containing archaeon Methanothermus fervidus (see Materials and methods). Comparing M. fervidus to T. acidophilum, we find a very similar nested, edge-aligned structure of smaller fragments within broader peaks (Figure 4e,h).
evidence: This is supported by MNase-seq data analysis shown in Figure 4e,h.

claim: In M. fervidus, the nested, edge-aligned pattern is consistent with oligomerization in dimer steps from the minimal histone tetramer.
source: In M. fervidus, this pattern is consistent with oligomerization, in dimer steps, from the minimal histone tetramer (Maruyama et al., 2013; Mattiroli et al., 2017).
evidence: This is inferred from the data and supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Both broad and narrow HTa peaks exhibit relatively elevated GC content at their center and are flanked by short stretches of GC depletion.
source: At a coarse level, we find that both broad and narrow peaks exhibit relatively elevated GC content at their center and are flanked by short stretches of GC depletion (Figure 4i,j).
evidence: This is supported by nucleotide composition analysis shown in Figure 4i,j.

claim: A specific binding motif is not evident for HTa.
source: In line with promiscuous binding, a specific binding motif, as one would observe for most transcription factors, is not evident (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by motif analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: For broader peaks, peak-internal GC content positively tracks small fragment abundance in both T. acidophilum and M. fervidus.
source: For broader peaks, it is worth noting that, in both T. acidophilum and M. fervidus, once we have re-oriented the small fragment coverage signal as described above, peak-internal GC content positively tracks small fragment abundance (Figure 4j,k), supporting a model where nucleation happens on more GC-rich sites whereas sequence need not be as favorable for subsequent extension events.
evidence: This is supported by analysis shown in Figure 4j,k.

claim: Narrow peaks where large fragments are rare tend to be flanked by more AT-rich sequence in both T. acidophilum and M. fervidus.
source: Note, however, that while sequence might be more important for nucleation than extension, it is by no means irrelevant for the latter: narrow peaks where large fragments are rare tend to be flanked by more AT-rich sequence in both T. acidophilum and M. fervidus, suggesting that sequence can prevent or at least predispose against oligomer formation (Figure 4—figure supplements 2–3).
evidence: This is supported by analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplements 2–3.

claim: HTa-bound reads show a short central track of reduced GC enrichment that is symmetric around the HTa/nucleosome dyad.
source: Read-internal dinucleotide profiles confirm an overall GC preference but also reveal local enrichment/depletion patterns, notably a short central track of reduced GC enrichment (Figure 5a) in T. acidophilum as well as histone-encoding archaea, which is symmetric around the HTa/nucleosome dyad.
evidence: This is supported by dinucleotide frequency analysis shown in Figure 5a.

claim: HTa-bound reads show mononucleotide and RR/YY profiles similar to those previously observed for eukaryotic histones.
source: Unexpectedly, we also find mononucleotide and RR/YY (R = A or G; Y = T or C) profiles similar to those previously observed for – and attributed to the unique geometry of – eukaryotic histones (Reynolds et al., 2010; Ioshikhes et al., 2011; Quintales et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by nucleotide frequency analysis and citations to prior work on eukaryotic histones.

claim: HTa-bound reads show mononucleotide and RR/YY profiles with strong counter-phasing and asymmetry across the dyad.
source: These profiles show strong counter-phasing and asymmetry across the dyad (Figure 5b,c) and are particularly prominent in T. acidophilum and Thermococcus kodakarensis.
evidence: This is supported by nucleotide frequency analysis shown in Figure 5b,c.

claim: Symmetric and asymmetric nucleotide enrichments across a dyad axis are not limited to nucleosomes.
source: These observations suggest that symmetric and asymmetric nucleotide enrichments across a dyad axis are not limited to nucleosomes and, furthermore, imply that the HTa-DNA complex is symmetric.
evidence: This is inferred from the nucleotide frequency patterns observed for HTa.

claim: The HTa-DNA complex is symmetric.
source: These observations suggest that symmetric and asymmetric nucleotide enrichments across a dyad axis are not limited to nucleosomes and, furthermore, imply that the HTa-DNA complex is symmetric.
evidence: This is inferred from the symmetric nucleotide enrichment patterns.

claim: LASSO models trained on small and large fragments confirm a general enrichment for strong (S = G or C) over weak (W = A or T) nucleotides.
source: To define nucleotide preferences more rigorously and enable prediction of relative occupancy from underlying nucleotide features, as previously done for eukaryotic histones (Tillo and Hughes, 2009), we trained Lasso models on small and large fragments separately (see Materials and methods). The models confirm a general enrichment for strong (S = G or C) over weak (W = A or T) nucleotides, with mono- and dinucleotide frequencies the strongest individual predictors (Figure 5e).
evidence: This is supported by LASSO modeling results shown in Figure 5e.

claim: Mono- and dinucleotide frequencies are the strongest individual predictors in LASSO models for HTa occupancy.
source: The models confirm a general enrichment for strong (S = G or C) over weak (W = A or T) nucleotides, with mono- and dinucleotide frequencies the strongest individual predictors (Figure 5e).
evidence: This is supported by LASSO modeling results shown in Figure 5e.

claim: For small fragments, predicted and observed occupancy are well correlated (ρ(day 2)=0.76; ρ(day 3.5)=0.86).
source: For small fragments, predicted and observed occupancy are well correlated (ρ(day 2)=0.76; ρ(day 3.5)=0.86, observed versus predicted in test set, p<2.2e-16, Figure 5d).
evidence: This is supported by LASSO model predictions shown in Figure 5d.

claim: Fragment ends from naked T. acidophilum genomic DNA exhibit the expected MNase cutting bias.
source: First, we digested, sequenced, and analyzed naked genomic DNA from T. acidophilum. Fragment ends exhibit the expected MNase cutting bias and subtly higher GC than the genomic average (Figure 5f).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of naked DNA digest shown in Figure 5f.

claim: The read-internal nucleotide enrichment patterns observed in native chromatin digests are absent from naked DNA.
source: Importantly, however, the read-internal nucleotide enrichment patterns we observe in native chromatin digests (Figure 5a–c) are absent from naked DNA (Figure 5f), read coverage along the genome is poorly correlated between naked DNA and native chromatin (ρ = 0.07, p<2.2e-16, Figure 5g), and a Lasso model trained on naked DNA fails to predict occupancy in vivo (Figure 5—figure supplement 2, ρ = −0.04, p<2.2e-16).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of naked DNA and native chromatin data shown in Figure 5f.

claim: Read coverage along the genome is poorly correlated between naked DNA and native chromatin (ρ = 0.07, p<2.2e-16).
source: Importantly, however, the read-internal nucleotide enrichment patterns we observe in native chromatin digests (Figure 5a–c) are absent from naked DNA (Figure 5f), read coverage along the genome is poorly correlated between naked DNA and native chromatin (ρ = 0.07, p<2.2e-16, Figure 5g), and a Lasso model trained on naked DNA fails to predict occupancy in vivo (Figure 5—figure supplement 2, ρ = −0.04, p<2.2e-16).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 5g.

claim: A Lasso model trained on naked DNA fails to predict occupancy in vivo (ρ = −0.04, p<2.2e-16).
source: Importantly, however, the read-internal nucleotide enrichment patterns we observe in native chromatin digests (Figure 5a–c) are absent from naked DNA (Figure 5f), read coverage along the genome is poorly correlated between naked DNA and native chromatin (ρ = 0.07, p<2.2e-16, Figure 5g), and a Lasso model trained on naked DNA fails to predict occupancy in vivo (Figure 5—figure supplement 2, ρ = −0.04, p<2.2e-16).
evidence: This is supported by LASSO modeling results shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Reads obtained from HTa-expressing E. coli exhibit internal nucleotide enrichments matching those in T. acidophilum.
source: Second, we surveyed digest fragments obtained from HTa-expressing E. coli and compared them to fragments from an E. coli genomic DNA digest. Reads obtained from the HTa-expressing strain exhibit internal nucleotide enrichments matching those in T. acidophilum. Reads from the genomic DNA do not (Figure 5f).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of E. coli HTa-expressing and genomic DNA digests shown in Figure 5f.

claim: Reads from E. coli genomic DNA digest do not exhibit internal nucleotide enrichments matching those in T. acidophilum.
source: Reads obtained from the HTa-expressing strain exhibit internal nucleotide enrichments matching those in T. acidophilum. Reads from the genomic DNA do not (Figure 5f).
evidence: This is supported by analysis shown in Figure 5f.

claim: Reads from an E. coli native chromatin digest do not exhibit internal nucleotide enrichments matching those in T. acidophilum.
source: Neither do reads from an E. coli native chromatin digest (Rojec et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Coverage of small fragments in vitro and in vivo is well correlated (ρ = 0.61, p<2.2e-16).
source: Coverage of small fragments in vitro and in vivo is well correlated (Figure 6a, ρ = 0.61, p<2.2e-16) and the Lasso model trained on the in vitro data predicts occupancy in vivo (Figure 6b, ρ = 0.68, p<2.2e-16).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 6a.

claim: The Lasso model trained on in vitro reconstitution data predicts occupancy in vivo (ρ = 0.68, p<2.2e-16).
source: Coverage of small fragments in vitro and in vivo is well correlated (Figure 6a, ρ = 0.61, p<2.2e-16) and the Lasso model trained on the in vitro data predicts occupancy in vivo (Figure 6b, ρ = 0.68, p<2.2e-16).
evidence: This is supported by LASSO modeling results shown in Figure 6b.

claim: 42% of the variance in occupancy in vivo is explained by sequence preferences in vitro.
source: This is consistent with a major role for sequence in driving positioning of HTa in vivo, with 42% of the variance in occupancy in vivo explained by sequence preferences in vitro.
evidence: This is calculated from the correlation coefficient (ρ = 0.68) between in vitro predictions and in vivo occupancy.

claim: Addition of HTa retards the migration of a subset of dsDNA oligos in a concentration-dependent manner.
source: Addition of HTa retards the migration of a subset of dsDNA oligos in a concentration-dependent manner (Figure 6c,d).
evidence: This is supported by EMSA data shown in Figure 6c,d.

claim: At high HTa:DNA mass ratios, the majority of oligos are subject to retardation.
source: At high HTa:DNA mass ratios, the majority of oligos are subject to retardation, as expected from proteins that, like histones, have compositional preferences but are capable of binding most sequences.
evidence: This is supported by EMSA data and comparison to histone behavior.

claim: Pslow is positively correlated with GC content in EMSA experiments.
source: For the remaining oligos, we then ask if Pslow varies as a function of nucleotide content, as predicted by our MNase-Seq data. We find this to be the case. Pslow is positively correlated with GC content (Figure 6e, Figure 6—figure supplement 3) and, even more strikingly, with the number of GpC dinucleotides in the oligo (Figure 6f, Figure 6—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by EMSA-seq analysis shown in Figure 6e and Figure 6—figure supplement 3.

claim: Pslow is positively correlated with the number of GpC dinucleotides in the oligo.
source: Pslow is positively correlated with GC content (Figure 6e, Figure 6—figure supplement 3) and, even more strikingly, with the number of GpC dinucleotides in the oligo (Figure 6f, Figure 6—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by EMSA-seq analysis shown in Figure 6f and Figure 6—figure supplement 4.

claim: GpC dinucleotide content is the strongest individual predictor in Lasso models for in vivo chromatin occupancy.
source: The latter is noteworthy because GpC dinucleotide content is the strongest individual predictor in Lasso models for in vivo chromatin occupancy (Figure 5e).
evidence: This is supported by LASSO modeling results shown in Figure 5e.

claim: The Lasso model trained on in vivo chromatin predicts small fragment occupancy across the growth cycle well (ρ > 0.7).
source: As demonstrated above, the Lasso model trained on in vivo chromatin predicts small fragment occupancy across the growth cycle well (ρ > 0.7, Figure 5e).
evidence: This is supported by LASSO modeling results shown in Figure 5e.

claim: The Lasso model trained on in vivo chromatin performs much worse when trying to predict large fragment coverage in exponential phase (ρ = 0.43, p<2.2e-16).
source: Curiously, it performs much worse when trying to predict large fragment coverage in exponential phase (Figure 5e, day 2, ρ = 0.43, p<2.2e-16).
evidence: This is supported by LASSO modeling results shown in Figure 5e.

claim: Broad peaks where small fragments are rarest show strongly divergent sequence composition.
source: To explore this hypothesis, we divided broad peaks into deciles based on the relative coverage of small fragments at these peaks. Doing so, we find that broad peaks where small fragments are rarest show strongly divergent sequence composition (Figure 7a).
evidence: This is supported by sequence composition analysis shown in Figure 7a.

claim: Divergent broad peaks are common in exponential phase but disappear almost entirely in stationary phase.
source: These divergent peaks are common in exponential phase, but disappear almost entirely in stationary phase, which is dominated by broad peaks that conform to the nucleation-extension model instead (Figure 7b, Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by analysis across growth phases shown in Figure 7b and Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Broad peaks with few small fragments are particularly enriched in intergenic sequence (hypergeometric test p<2.2e-16).
source: Broad peaks with few small fragments are particularly enriched in intergenic sequence (Figure 8a, hypergeometric test p<2.2e-16), and it is around transcriptional start sites (TSSs, Figure 8b; approximated from RNA-seq data, see Materials and methods) and end sites (TESs, Figure 8—figure supplement 1), where their disappearance in stationary phase is most striking (Figure 8b).
evidence: This is supported by genomic location analysis shown in Figure 8a.

claim: No equivalent to independent large fragments is found in histone-encoding archaea.
source: We find no equivalent to these independent large fragments in histone-encoding archaea (Figure 8c–e, Figure 8—figure supplement 1) suggesting that they are specific to T. acidophilum.
evidence: This is supported by comparison with MNase-seq data from histone-encoding archaea shown in Figure 8c–e and Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: Independent large fragments are specific to T. acidophilum.
source: We find no equivalent to these independent large fragments in histone-encoding archaea (Figure 8c–e, Figure 8—figure supplement 1) suggesting that they are specific to T. acidophilum.
evidence: This is inferred from comparison with other archaea.

claim: Neither in vitro reconstitution nor HTa expression in E. coli yielded independent large fragments similar to those in T. acidophilum.
source: Neither in vitro reconstitution nor HTa expression in E. coli yielded similar independent fragments.
evidence: This is based on analysis of in vitro and E. coli expression data.

claim: Independent large fragments likely reflect the binding of different proteins or protein complexes in T. acidophilum whose identity remains to be established.
source: It is therefore parsimonious to conclude that these fragments likely reflect the binding of different proteins or protein complexes in T. acidophilum whose identity remains to be established.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that these fragments are not produced by HTa alone.

claim: The disappearance of independent fragments in stationary phase is not obviously coupled to local changes in transcription.
source: Importantly, even though their positioning suggests that they might be involved in gene regulation, the disappearance of independent fragments in stationary phase is not obviously coupled to local changes in transcription: the abundance of independent fragments drops in similar fashion for genes that are up- or down-regulated or remain the same in stationary compared to exponential phase (Figure 8f).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of fragment abundance and transcription changes shown in Figure 8f.

claim: The relative abundance of smaller fragments around transcriptional start sites appears entirely insensitive to changes in transcription.
source: At the same time, the relative abundance of smaller fragments around transcriptional start sites appears entirely insensitive to changes in transcription (Figure 8f), and thus provides no support for a role of HTa in the dynamic regulation of transcription.
evidence: This is supported by analysis shown in Figure 8f.

claim: HTa is a protein of bacterial origin that converged onto supramolecular properties reminiscent of archaeal histones.
source: The evidence above suggests that HTa is a protein of bacterial origin that converged onto supramolecular properties reminiscent of archaeal histones.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from all the experimental evidence presented.

claim: Well-characterized HU homologs exhibit elevated occupancy in AT-rich regions, prefer an AT-rich motif at the center of the binding footprint, or bind sequence non-selectively.
source: Whereas well-characterized HU homologs exhibit elevated occupancy in AT-rich regions, prefer an AT-rich motif at the center of the binding footprint, or bind sequence non-selectively (Swinger and Rice, 2007; Grove, 2011; Prieto et al., 2012), HTa shows a more histone-like preference for GC and even exhibits asymmetric mononucleotide/RR/YY profiles across the dyad.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work on HU proteins.

claim: HTa shows a more histone-like preference for GC than well-characterized HU homologs.
source: Whereas well-characterized HU homologs exhibit elevated occupancy in AT-rich regions, prefer an AT-rich motif at the center of the binding footprint, or bind sequence non-selectively (Swinger and Rice, 2007; Grove, 2011; Prieto et al., 2012), HTa shows a more histone-like preference for GC and even exhibits asymmetric mononucleotide/RR/YY profiles across the dyad.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing GC preference of HTa.

claim: HTa exhibits asymmetric mononucleotide/RR/YY profiles across the dyad.
source: Whereas well-characterized HU homologs exhibit elevated occupancy in AT-rich regions, prefer an AT-rich motif at the center of the binding footprint, or bind sequence non-selectively (Swinger and Rice, 2007; Grove, 2011; Prieto et al., 2012), HTa shows a more histone-like preference for GC and even exhibits asymmetric mononucleotide/RR/YY profiles across the dyad.
evidence: This is supported by nucleotide frequency analysis.

claim: HTa can be regarded as an archaeal histone analog.
source: Based on these observations, we propose that HTa can be regarded as an archaeal histone analog.
evidence: This is the main proposal of the paper based on all the evidence presented.

claim: Structural work will be required to characterize how HTa interacts with DNA.
source: This analogy is, of course, preliminary. Structural work will be required to characterize how HTa interacts with DNA and to determine whether large HTa-protected fragments reflect closely spaced binding events or, in further analogy to archaeal histones, the presence of contiguous HTa polymers.
evidence: This is a statement about future work needed.

claim: Even larger protected fragments can be formed when HTa is expressed in E. coli.
source: The observation that even larger protected fragments can be formed when HTa is expressed in E. coli (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) or reconstituted in vitro (Figure 6—figure supplement 1) is interesting in this regard and deserves further exploration.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Even larger protected fragments can be formed when HTa is reconstituted in vitro.
source: The observation that even larger protected fragments can be formed when HTa is expressed in E. coli (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) or reconstituted in vitro (Figure 6—figure supplement 1) is interesting in this regard and deserves further exploration.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: HTa facilitates re-annealing following DNA denaturation.
source: Searcy and co-workers showed that HTa facilitates re-annealing following DNA denaturation (Stein and Searcy, 1978), suggesting that HTa might assist DNA renaturation after thermal stress.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: E. coli HU, when added to naked DNA, significantly raises its melting temperature.
source: However, the physiological importance of HTa-mediated reannealing remains to be established and is put into perspective by the observation that E. coli HU, when added to naked DNA, also significantly raises its melting temperature (Drlica and Rouviere-Yaniv, 1987).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Dinoflagellates represent a second case where histones have lost their pre-eminent role in genome compaction and organization to other small basic proteins.
source: Finally, from an evolutionary perspective, it is worth highlighting dinoflagellates as a second case where histones have lost their pre-eminent role in genome compaction and organization to other small basic proteins.
evidence: This is established knowledge about dinoflagellates.

claim: Histones remain encoded in dinoflagellate genomes.
source: Even though histones remain encoded in dinoflagellate genomes (Marinov and Lynch, 2016), and might continue to play important roles in transcription or other processes, they are no longer the main protein constituent of chromatin.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Proteins with homologs in phycodnaviruses have become the principal mediators of compaction in dinoflagellates.
source: Instead, proteins with homologs in phycodnaviruses have become the principal mediators of compaction (Gornik et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: In a subset of dinoflagellate species, dinoflagellate/viral nucleoproteins (DVNPs) act alongside HU-like proteins that were likely acquired from bacteria.
source: In a subset of species, these dinoflagellate/viral nucleoproteins (DVNPs) act alongside HU-like proteins that were likely acquired from bacteria (Figure 2a) (Wong et al., 2003; Janouškovec et al., 2017) and might be involved in the genesis and maintenance of DNA loop structures (Chan and Wong, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work and phylogenetic data in Figure 2a.

claim: HU proteins are versatile, evolvable and have been independently co-opted into important chromatin architectural roles following horizontal transfer.
source: If not exactly a precedent, the case of dinoflagellates nonetheless serves to illustrate that HU proteins are versatile, evolvable and have been independently co-opted into important chromatin architectural roles following horizontal transfer.
evidence: This is inferred from the examples of HTa and dinoflagellates.

claim: Histones or a subset of their functions can be replaced, under the right circumstances, by alternative DNA-binding proteins with fundamentally different folds.
source: It also highlights that histones or a subset of their functions can be replaced, under the right circumstances, by alternative DNA-binding proteins with fundamentally different folds.
evidence: This is inferred from the examples presented.

claim: Histone replacements need not necessarily go hand in hand with fundamental changes to the architectural layout of chromatin.
source: At the same time, our results demonstrate that such replacements, even though they appear radical, need not necessarily go hand in hand with fundamental changes to the architectural layout of chromatin.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that HTa shows histone-like chromatin organization despite being structurally different.
